fichas.title: Possible arrangements of service shafts, columns and vertical circulation cores
fichas.summary: Illustrates six laboratory-building arrangements combining service shafts and vertical circulation cores: joint shafts on the building face with an internal core; external joint shafts with an external core; central joint shafts with the core as a leading element; distributed single-shaft installations with an internal core; internal installation coupled with the core; and external shafts with a central core in a cruciform plan.
uses: Organizing vertical building services and circulation in laboratory buildings

fichas.title: Vertical services system for laboratories
fichas.summary: Many vertical supply lines run in individual shafts, internally or on the façade, carrying services to laboratories. Air supply and extraction ducts to fume cupboards are routed decentrally, with separate roof ventilators. This arrangement offers maximum individual supply and short horizontal connections to laboratory benches, but limits floor-layout flexibility and requires more space on working and services floors.
uses: Supplying laboratory services through individual vertical shafts
Connecting services horizontally to laboratory benches and fume cupboards

fichas.title: Horizontal services system and joint service shaft
fichas.summary: Vertical main services for all media are concentrated in joint shafts and distributed horizontally through services floors, connecting to laboratory benches from above or below. The arrangement uses less space in service shafts and allows greater floor-layout flexibility, simpler maintenance, central ventilation equipment, and better adaptability. High installation density requires substantial space. The page illustrates horizontal conduits and ducts in ceiling space and a joint-shaft plan. Conduits should be insulated against condensation, heat, cold, and noise transmission.
uses: Distributing building services horizontally from joint vertical shafts
Routing air supply and exhaust through ceiling space

Vertical services system --7 0
Many vertical supply lines, internally or on the fac;:ade, run the
media in individual shafts to the laboratories. Decentrally routed
air supply and extraction ducts to the fume cupboards, separate
ventilators on the roof.
Advantage: maximum individual supply; short horizontal connections to laboratory bench.
Disadvantage: limited floor layout flexibility; greater space requirement on working and services floors.
Horizontal services system --7 Cl!>:
Vertical main services for all media concentrated in joint shafts
and distributed horizontally from there into the services floors with
upper or lower connection to laboratory benches.
Advantages: less space required in the services shafts, greater
flexibility of floor layout, simpler maintenance, central ventilation
equipment, better adaptability. High density of installation requires
large amount of space. Vertical joint shafts are simpler, more
accessible and allow revisions.
Conduits should be insulated against condensation, heat, cold
